frompp: ខ្ញុំមកពីភ្នំពេញ។

hello: Use this candidate for a casual meeting between adults of similar age. Review the greeting and setting together; this is not a universal address rule.
You meet a friend of your partner. Offer a casual hello.
formal: Keep the formal greeting distinct from the casual scene. A fluent reviewer must confirm when it fits; recognition here is not a cultural etiquette assessment.
You need to recognize the formal greeting from this lesson.
thanks: Use this after someone helps you. It acknowledges help rather than asking for new information.
Someone repeats their name for you. Thank them.
sorry: This candidate marks an apology or excuse me. Review the situation and intonation before recording it; it does not itself ask for repetition.
Politely get someone’s attention before asking for help.
nameq: The draft scene uses adults of similar age. The address choice needs fluent review; do not generalize it to every relationship or formal meeting.
Ask the person you just met for their name.
alex: Alex is the name assigned in this practice scene. Replace the name when speaking for yourself; the app only checks the authored choices.
You are playing Alex. Say what your name is.
sam: Sam is a different practice name. Keep the name asked for in view; both name sentences are possible in other situations.
You are playing Sam. Introduce yourself.
fromq: This asks about origin in the draft scene. It is a different request from asking for someone’s name. The colloquial wording needs contemporary review.
Ask where your new acquaintance is from.
frompp: The assigned practice detail is Phnom Penh. This does not imply where any actual learner lives or comes from.
Your practice character is from Phnom Penh. Share that detail.
fromus: The assigned practice detail is America. The place-name wording and help are provisional; a reviewer must confirm them.
Your practice character is from America. Share that detail.
repeat: Use the repetition request when you missed the words. It is distinct from a request to change speed. The script/help is an original modern candidate informed by a historical pattern, pending fluent review.
You missed a name. Ask the person to say it again.
slow: Use the speed request when the words came too quickly. This modern script/help candidate needs fluent review; the historical reference does not approve it.
You heard the words but the pace was too fast. Ask for slower speech.

lessons.title: Greet someone
lessons.goal: Greet a peer and thank them for their welcome.
lessons.scenario: Your partner introduces you to a friend of a similar age at their home. Greet each other, introduce yourselves, then thank the host for welcoming you.
lessons.usage: Keep the greeting, thank-you and attention-getter attached to their situations. The formal greeting is a recognition contrast; this casual scene does not require it.
practice: Your peer has just greeted you. Return the casual greeting taught in this scene.
Your host helped you join the conversation. Thank them.
You need to get someone’s attention before your question. Choose the attention-getter.
You are reading a note labeled “formal greeting.” Select the matching expression, rather than a thank-you or an apology.
At the end of the welcome, the host helps with your coat. Acknowledge that help.
In the hallway, get a person’s attention before a question. Choose the expression that does that.

lessons.title: Introduce yourself
lessons.goal: Give your name and ask someone else’s name.
lessons.scenario: You are Alex, meeting Sam through a friend. You are both adults of a similar age. Use the assigned names in this practice.
lessons.usage: Keep your assigned name separate from the other person’s name. A name question calls for a name; an origin question calls for a place. Address and name spacing remain review items.
practice: Sam asks your name. You are playing Alex. Give your own name.
You have introduced yourself. Ask Sam for their name.
Alex asks your name. You are now playing Sam. Give the name assigned to you.
You missed the name on a written introduction card. Which expression asks for a name?
A written profile asks for the name Alex. Choose the matching self-introduction, not the other person’s name.
At another meeting you are Sam. Alex has introduced themself; ask the name question yourself.

lessons.title: Get to know each other
lessons.goal: Exchange a name and one simple personal detail.
lessons.scenario: At a small gathering, Alex is from America and Sam is from Phnom Penh. These are assigned practice details, not assumptions about you.
lessons.usage: Choose the detail the question asks for. Reuse the introduction pattern in a new meeting rather than treating a name and an origin as interchangeable answers.
practice: You know Sam’s name. Ask about their origin next.
Alex asks where you are from. You are Sam, whose assigned origin is Phnom Penh.
Sam asks the same question. You are Alex, whose assigned origin is America.
At a later introduction you are asked for your name, not your origin. You are Alex.
In an introduction message, give only the assigned origin America rather than a name or a different origin.
A friend has introduced themselves as Alex. Ask the origin question next, rather than repeating the name question.

lessons.title: Ask for help understanding
lessons.goal: Ask for repetition or slower speech, then respond.
lessons.scenario: In a noisy room you miss Sam’s name. Ask for help, read the repeated line, then respond. No listening is required in this text candidate.
lessons.usage: A request to repeat asks for the words again; a speed request asks for a slower delivery. After clarification, respond to the actual information. These requests need contemporary script, pronunciation and politeness review before use as teaching models.
practice: You missed Sam’s name. Ask to hear it again.
The person is speaking too fast. Ask them to slow down.
Sam repeats their name to help you. Thank them.
The question has now been clarified: it asks for your name. You are Alex. Answer it.
A chair scrapes across the floor while the name is said. Request the words again.
At a later table a different person is speaking too fast. Ask specifically for a change of pace.

lessons.title: Keep the exchange going
lessons.goal: Greet someone, exchange details and repair a missed question.
lessons.scenario: A different gathering: you are Sam and meet Alex at a friend’s home. Use earlier phrases in a changed role and clarify when needed.
lessons.usage: Use the earlier phrases in a new role. Answer a name question with a name and an origin question with a place. Ask for clarification whenever it helps; needing help does not prevent finishing.
practice: At the doorway, return a peer’s casual greeting before you exchange details.
You are Sam at this gathering. Give your assigned name.
Alex asks where you are from. Your assigned origin is Phnom Penh.
You missed the next question. Ask for repetition instead of guessing an answer.
You can read the clarified question: it asks for your name. You are Sam.
At the next table the pace is too fast. Ask for slower speech.
